claims.text: Conventional spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu composites exhibit high interfacial thermal resistance.
Introducing a carbon-containing atmosphere during spark plasma sintering at approximately 1000°C will form WC in situ at W–Cu interfaces.
Controlled carburization will produce a nanometric WC interphase localized at W–Cu boundaries.
An ultrathin WC interphase enhances electron–phonon coupling across a W–Cu interface.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling across the interface reduces thermal boundary resistance.
Reducing W–Cu thermal boundary resistance increases the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
The inherent hardness of WC helps the carburized composite maintain mechanical strength.
The chemical stability of WC helps the composite resist irradiation-induced damage.
Controlled carburization will give W–Cu composites higher effective thermal conductivity than otherwise comparable non-carburized W–Cu composites.
The conductivity increase will occur without a reduction in mechanical durability.
The conductivity increase will occur without a reduction in irradiation resistance.
An overly thick WC interphase may embrittle the composite.
A discontinuous WC interphase may embrittle the composite.
The intervention is effective only when carburization is precisely controlled.
Approximately 1000°C represents standard SPS conditions applicable to this intervention.
The proposed composite is intended to operate at approximately 300–600°C in fusion-reactor joint environments.
Fusion-reactor component environments involve high temperatures and high heat flux.
Resistance to irradiation is an important requirement for materials used in fusion-reactor environments.
Ion irradiation can simulate the fusion-reactor irradiation conditions relevant to evaluating the proposed composite.
